commons:60945135.summary: On the swelling body of this tall silver flask, partly gilded, the archangel Gabriel strides ahead leading the three Magi with their gifts toward the Christ Child, who sits on his mother's lap beneath the guiding star. Flasks of this kind may have been used as containers in a church, and the Magi were a favourite subject on early Byzantine objects linked to pilgrimage.
facts: The Met notes that only the Armenian Infancy Gospel describes the archangel as the Magi's guide.
commons:60945135.notes: The relief is too small in the thumbnail to confirm details; description follows the Met. 'c' set only to the Met's 'Byzantine' culture; no place of manufacture is given.

vam:O363613.summary: This fragment of an embroidered roundel shows a row of haloed men, one of them white-haired, ranged behind a curved table edged with a row of round shapes. Below, a servant in a short tunic carries a jug on his shoulder, and a border of heart-shaped flowers and rosettes on a green ground encloses the scene. The V&A identifies the subject as the Last Supper; the semicircular table follows the way Christ's meal with his disciples was pictured in early Christian art, though the figure of Christ himself cannot be picked out on what survives.
facts: The roundel was originally stitched to a linen tunic, and a fragment of the plain undyed tunic remains attached to it.
It was purchased in 1903, together with V&A objects 813 to 820-1903, from L. Paul Philip in Cairo, for £80.
vam:O363613.notes: Identification as the Last Supper follows the V&A. Christ is not clearly identifiable on the fragment (the end of the table, where he is usually placed, is partly lost), and the servant carrying a jug could also suit another meal scene such as the Wedding at Cana. Scripture omitted for this reason.
